request.subject: Semiconductor industry
request.question: Produce a research report on the semiconductor industry: market size and growth, key competitors and their positioning (compute/AI accelerators, foundry, memory, equipment), industry drivers, and material risks (cyclicality, export controls, concentration, valuation). Use primary sources (SIA/WSTS, company IR releases, TSMC, BIS) and the Anthropic sector-overview / competitive-analysis method.

executive_summary: On the caller-supplied primary releases, the semiconductor industry is in an AI- and memory-led upcycle of exceptional magnitude. SIA reports Q3 2026 global sales of $517.7bn, up 24.1% QoQ, and September 2026 (3-month moving average) sales up 146.8% YoY. WSTS's Q2 update of its spring forecast puts 2026 at about $1,655bn (+~108%) and 2027 at about $2.1tn (+~29%), with memory up ~302% in 2026. Company prints corroborate the direction: NVIDIA Q2 FY27 revenue $96.2bn (+105.9% YoY, Data Center 92.5% of revenue, 66.2% GAAP operating margin), TSMC 3Q26 revenue $46.72bn (+41.2% YoY, 66.4% gross margin, 79% of wafer revenue at 7nm and below), Micron FQ4-26 revenue $54.23bn (+379% YoY) and AMD Q3 2026 revenue $13.38bn (+45%). All four guide to further sequential growth (TSMC midpoint +14.1%, NVIDIA +12.2%, AMD +27.1%, Micron +13.4%). A key analytical point: the WSTS full-year 2026 figure is already too low on its own arithmetic — it implies Q4 sales of only $435.3bn, 15.9% below SIA's Q3 actual, while the companies guide up — so the WSTS autumn forecast (conference Nov 16-19, 2026) is the next reference-setting data point. Material risks are a memory-price-driven cycle (memory growth far outruns logic), concentration of leading-edge supply in TSMC and of demand in AI data-center capex, US export controls that NVIDIA already excludes from guidance for China data-center compute, and valuation, which this run could not assess because no market-price source was available. All sourced figures are PROVISIONAL (caller-supplied, not re-fetched in this run); several magnitudes are far outside historical industry ranges and should be re-verified against the original documents before reliance.

key_findings.finding: Industry revenue is growing at a pace without modern precedent: SIA Q3 2026 sales $517.7bn (+24.1% QoQ), September 3MMA sales $172.6bn (+146.8% YoY); WSTS calculates 2026 at ~$1,655bn (+~108%) and 2027 at ~$2.1tn (+~29%). Q1-Q3 2026 cumulative sales are $1,219.7bn (WSTS H1 $702bn + SIA Q3). The September 3MMA x3 ($517.8bn) ties to the Q3 total within rounding.

Memory is the swing factor of this cycle. WSTS expects memory to grow ~302% in 2026, versus ~108% for the total market; Micron's FQ4-26 revenue of $54.23bn is 4.8x the year-earlier $11.32bn (+379.1%), +30.8% QoQ, and FY2026 revenue was $133.19bn, with FQ1-27 guided to $61.5bn ±$1.5bn (+13.4% at midpoint). Growth this concentrated in a historically price-driven commodity segment makes the aggregate market more cyclical, not less.

The WSTS full-year 2026 figure is internally inconsistent with the run-rate: $1,655bn less H1 $702bn less SIA Q3 $517.7bn leaves an implied Q4 of $435.3bn, 15.9% below Q3. Every company in the sample guides Q4/next quarter up sequentially (TSMC +14.1% at midpoint, NVIDIA +12.2%, AMD +27.1%, Micron +13.4%). Either WSTS's spring-based calculation understates 2026, or a sharp Q4 correction is embedded; the WSTS autumn forecast (Nov 16-19, 2026) should resolve this. Implied quarterly path from the same sources: Q1 ~$284.8bn, Q2 ~$417.2bn, Q3 $517.7bn.

Compute/AI accelerators: NVIDIA is the dominant scale player — Q2 FY27 revenue $96.22bn (+105.9% YoY), Data Center $89.0bn (92.5% of revenue), GAAP gross margin 75.0% and GAAP operating margin 66.2%, Q3 FY27 outlook $108.0bn ±2% (+12.2% sequential) while assuming no China data-center compute revenue. AMD is the principal merchant challenger at roughly one-seventh of NVIDIA's quarterly revenue ($13.38bn, +45% YoY, 54% GAAP / 56% non-GAAP gross margin) but guides faster sequential growth (Q4 ~$17bn, +27.1%). Fiscal periods differ (NVIDIA quarter ended July 2026; AMD September 2026).

Foundry: TSMC is the leading-edge bottleneck and is earning exceptional returns — 3Q26 revenue $46.72bn (+41.2% YoY, +16.2% QoQ), gross margin 66.4%, operating margin 58.7%; 79% of wafer revenue from 7nm and below (2nm 8%, 3nm 33%, 5nm 28%, 7nm 10%; node shares sum to 79%, tying to the reported total). 4Q26 guidance $52.3-54.3bn (midpoint $53.3bn, +14.1% QoQ) with 65-67% gross margin. TSMC's growth (+41%) is well below the market's (+~108%), consistent with memory, not logic wafers, driving most of the aggregate jump.

Export controls remain an active, moving variable rather than a settled regime: BIS moved to case-by-case license review for H200/MI325X-class exports to China (2026-01-13), issued enforcement guidance on advanced computing items for D:5/Macau-headquartered entities (2026-05-31), extended the Entity List to 50%-owned affiliates (2025-09-29), changed VEU status for foreign-owned fabs in China (2025-08-29) and rescinded the AI Diffusion Rule (2025-05-13). NVIDIA's outlook excluding China data-center compute shows the revenue at stake is already outside base guidance.

Equipment, Broadcom/custom silicon and Intel could not be profiled: no SEMI equipment-sales figure was found and Broadcom/Intel releases were not fetched. Valuation (P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales, historical ranges) could not be assessed because no price source was available. The competitive picture is therefore partial on two of the four requested segments and silent on valuation.

scenarios.name: bull
scenarios.narrative: AI data-center capex and memory pricing hold through 2027: companies deliver on guided sequential growth (TSMC +14%, NVIDIA +12%, AMD +27%, Micron +13%), WSTS revises 2026 above $1,655bn at its Nov 16-19 conference and 2027 tracks or exceeds ~$2.1tn; China licensing under the January 2026 case-by-case policy adds revenue not in NVIDIA's guidance.

scenarios.name: base
scenarios.narrative: Q4 2026 broadly flat to up on Q3 as guided by the logic and memory leaders, WSTS lifts 2026 toward the run-rate and forecasts decelerating but positive 2027 growth (~29% on its current calculation); export-control policy stays restrictive but stable.

scenarios.name: bear
scenarios.narrative: Memory supply catches up and prices reset — the segment that grew ~302% in 2026 contracts — while hyperscaler capex digestion slows accelerator orders; the WSTS-implied Q4 decline (−15.9% QoQ) becomes the template for 2027, and tighter export controls or entity-list extensions remove further China revenue.

risks.risk: Cyclicality / memory price reversal: memory growth (~302% in 2026) and Micron's +379% YoY quarter are price-led and historically mean-revert; a memory downturn alone could turn aggregate industry growth negative.

Demand concentration: NVIDIA's Data Center segment is 92.5% of its revenue, and accelerator, HBM and leading-edge foundry demand all rest on the same AI data-center capex cycle — a slowdown hits compute, foundry and memory simultaneously.

Supply concentration: 79% of TSMC wafer revenue is at 7nm and below; leading-edge logic for the main accelerator vendors runs through one foundry and one geography (Taiwan), a single-point geopolitical and operational exposure.

Export controls: BIS rules on advanced computing items (case-by-case China licensing, D:5/Macau enforcement guidance, Entity List 50% affiliates rule, VEU changes for China fabs) change frequently; NVIDIA already excludes China data-center compute from its outlook.

Valuation: could not be assessed in this run (no price source). After revenue doubling and record margins (NVIDIA 66.2% operating, TSMC 58.7%), the risk is that peak-cycle earnings are capitalised as durable; multiples must be checked before any conclusion.

Data reliability: all figures come from a caller-supplied pack not re-fetched in this run, and the magnitudes (market +~108%, September +146.8% YoY) are far outside historical industry ranges; a transcription or retrieval error would change the conclusions.

counterarguments: The WSTS-implied Q4 decline may be an artefact of a spring forecast mechanically updated with Q2 actuals rather than a real signal; company guidance points the other way.

TSMC's +41.2% YoY growth is far below the market's ~108%, so the logic/foundry layer is growing much more modestly than the headline — the headline is heavily memory-price-driven and overstates volume growth.
Margins at NVIDIA (75% gross) and TSMC (66.4% gross) reflect scarcity pricing; new capacity (foundry, HBM) and AMD/custom-silicon competition could compress them even if volumes keep rising.

Export controls may loosen as well as tighten: the January 2026 case-by-case policy and the 2025 rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule show policy moving in both directions, so China is an upside as well as a downside variable.

implications.text: Treat the sector backdrop as an exceptionally strong but late-stage, memory-led upcycle with unresolved valuation. Any single-name opportunity in compute, foundry or memory should be evaluated with this report's cyclicality and concentration risks as the standing challenge, and with valuation work done separately once a price source is available.

Challenge points: (1) reconcile WSTS FY2026 $1,655bn with the SIA Q3 run-rate (implied Q4 −15.9% QoQ vs +12-27% guided by companies); (2) test how much of 2026 growth is memory price versus volume; (3) re-fetch S1-S6 to confirm the unusually large magnitudes before using them in any model; (4) stress the sector for a memory-price reset scenario.

The WSTS autumn forecast (Nov 16-19, 2026) is the next sector-level data point; NVIDIA's Q3 FY27 report and Micron's FQ1-27 report will test the guided sequential growth. Equipment, Broadcom/Intel and valuation are open gaps that a follow-up Merlin run with retrieval access can fill.
Use the cited figures (SIA, WSTS, TSMC, NVIDIA, AMD, Micron) as fundamental context; they are PROVISIONAL and fiscal periods differ by company.
